claim: Blood vessels are integrated into different organ environments with distinct properties and physiology.
source: Blood vessels are integrated into different organ environments with distinct properties and physiology (Augustin and Koh, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Augustin and Koh, 2017

claim: Certain molecular signals yield the opposite effect in bone vasculature as in other tissues.
source: A striking example of organ-specific specialization is the bone vasculature where certain molecular signals yield the opposite effect as in other tissues (Glomski et al., 2011; Kusumbe et al., 2014; Ramasamy et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Glomski et al., 2011; Kusumbe et al., 2014; Ramasamy et al., 2014

claim: Yap1 and Taz suppress vascular growth in the hypoxic microenvironment of bone.
source: Here, we show that the transcriptional coregulators Yap1 and Taz, components of the Hippo pathway, suppress vascular growth in the hypoxic microenvironment of bone, in contrast to their pro-angiogenic role in other organs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript including genetic mouse models and RNA sequencing

claim: Yap1 and Taz have a pro-angiogenic role in organs other than bone.
source: Here, we show that the transcriptional coregulators Yap1 and Taz, components of the Hippo pathway, suppress vascular growth in the hypoxic microenvironment of bone, in contrast to their pro-angiogenic role in other organs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in retina and citations to previous literature

claim: Lats2 is essential for bone angiogenesis.
source: Likewise, the kinase Lats2, which limits Yap1/Taz activity, is essential for bone angiogenesis but dispensable in organs with lower levels of hypoxia.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Lats2 mutant mice showing impaired bone angiogenesis

claim: Lats2 is dispensable for angiogenesis in organs with lower levels of hypoxia.
source: Likewise, the kinase Lats2, which limits Yap1/Taz activity, is essential for bone angiogenesis but dispensable in organs with lower levels of hypoxia.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing normal vasculature in other organs of Lats2 mutants

claim: Yap1/Taz constrain HIF1α target gene expression in vivo and in vitro.
source: With mouse genetics, RNA sequencing, biochemistry, and cell culture experiments, we show that Yap1/Taz constrain hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF1α) target gene expression in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data, ChIP experiments, and cell culture experiments presented in the manuscript

claim: Crosstalk between Yap1/Taz and HIF1α controls angiogenesis depending on the level of tissue hypoxia.
source: We propose that crosstalk between Yap1/Taz and HIF1α controls angiogenesis depending on the level of tissue hypoxia, resulting in organ-specific biological responses.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing differential effects in hypoxic vs normoxic tissues

claim: The local vasculature plays central roles in embryonic and postnatal bone development.
source: The local vasculature plays central roles in embryonic and postnatal bone development but also later in homeostasis and in repair processes (Gerber and Ferrara, 2000; Maes and Clemens, 2014; Zelzer and Olsen, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gerber and Ferrara, 2000; Maes and Clemens, 2014; Zelzer and Olsen, 2005

claim: Endochondral ossification requires the ingrowth of blood vessels into aggregates of hypertrophic chondrocytes.
source: Endochondral ossification and, in particular, the formation of ossification centers in the mouse embryo requires the ingrowth of blood vessels into aggregates of hypertrophic chondrocytes that express pro-angiogenic signals such as vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGF-A) (Eshkar-Oren et al., 2009; Maes et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eshkar-Oren et al., 2009; Maes et al., 2010

claim: Angiogenesis is essential for bone repair and regeneration.
source: The invasion of blood vessels also facilitates the entry of osteoblast precursors into fractured bone and, accordingly, angiogenesis is essential for bone repair and regeneration (Maes et al., 2010; Stegen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maes et al., 2010; Stegen et al., 2015

claim: Capillaries in bone are regionally and molecularly specialized.
source: It was also shown that capillaries in bone are regionally and molecularly specialized.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and data presented in the manuscript

claim: Type H endothelial cells express high levels of CD31 and Emcn.
source: Columnar vessels in the metaphysis and the capillaries of the endosteum, a connective tissue layer lining the inner surface of compact bone, are associated with osteoprogenitor cells expressing the transcription factor Osterix, express high levels of CD31 and Emcn (CD31hi Emcnhi), and have therefore been named type H.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kusumbe et al., 2014 and data presented in the manuscript

claim: Type L endothelial cells show comparably lower expression of CD31 and Emcn.
source: In contrast, the highly branched sinusoidal capillary network of the diaphysis shows comparably lower expression of the two markers (CD31lo Emcnlo or type L) and is predominantly associated with reticular mesenchymal cells and hematopoietic cells (Kusumbe et al., 2014; Ramasamy et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kusumbe et al., 2014; Ramasamy et al., 2016b

claim: Type E endothelial cells are abundant in embryonic and early postnatal long bones but gradually disappear in adolescent mice.
source: A further EC subpopulation with high CD31 expression – termed type E – is abundant in embryonic and early postnatal long bones but gradually disappears in adolescent mice (Langen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Langen et al., 2017

claim: Type H and type E but not type L ECs shift the differentiation of co-cultured primitive mesenchymal cells towards the osteoblast lineage.
source: Indicating that they are source of signals controlling the behavior of perivascular mesenchymal cells, type H and type E but not type L ECs shift the differentiation of co-cultured primitive mesenchymal cells towards the osteoblast lineage (Langen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Langen et al., 2017

claim: CD31hi Emcnhi ECs are strongly reduced in ovariectomized mice.
source: Interestingly, CD31hi Emcnhi ECs are strongly reduced in ovariectomized mice, a model of human postmenopausal osteoporosis, as well as in aging mice, which show an age-dependent decline in bone mineral density similar to human subjects (Kusumbe et al., 2014; Xie et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kusumbe et al., 2014; Xie et al., 2014

claim: Notch signaling in ECs promotes vessel growth in bone.
source: Notch and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling in ECs promote vessel growth in bone and help to maintain a functional type H EC population.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work

claim: HIF signaling in ECs promotes vessel growth in bone.
source: Notch and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) signaling in ECs promote vessel growth in bone and help to maintain a functional type H EC population.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work and data in the manuscript

claim: Activation of Notch and HIF pathways in the ECs of aged mice induces the reappearance of CD31hi Emcnhi together with perivascular Osterix-positive cells.
source: Activation of these pathways in the ECs of aged mice induces the reappearance of CD31hi Emcnhi together with perivascular Osterix-positive cells and is sufficient to increase the formation of mineralized bone in the metaphysis (Kusumbe et al., 2014; Ramasamy et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kusumbe et al., 2014; Ramasamy et al., 2016b

claim: Yap1 and Taz are transcriptional coactivators and key components of the Hippo pathway.
source: Yes-associated protein 1 (Yap1) and WW domain containing transcription regulator 1 (WWTR1), which is more widely known as Taz, are closely related transcriptional coactivators and key components of the Hippo pathway, an evolutionarily conserved signaling cascade controlling cell proliferation, differentiation and organ size (Dong et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2005 and established scientific knowledge

claim: The Hippo pathway is an evolutionarily conserved signaling cascade controlling cell proliferation, differentiation and organ size.
source: Yes-associated protein 1 (Yap1) and WW domain containing transcription regulator 1 (WWTR1), which is more widely known as Taz, are closely related transcriptional coactivators and key components of the Hippo pathway, an evolutionarily conserved signaling cascade controlling cell proliferation, differentiation and organ size (Dong et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dong et al., 2007; Huang et al., 2005 and established scientific knowledge

claim: Activation of Hippo signaling leads to exclusion of Yap1/Taz from the nucleus.
source: Activation of Hippo signaling leads to exclusion of Yap1/Taz from the nucleus and promotes the proteolytic degradation of these proteins.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations

claim: Activation of Hippo signaling promotes the proteolytic degradation of Yap1/Taz.
source: Activation of Hippo signaling leads to exclusion of Yap1/Taz from the nucleus and promotes the proteolytic degradation of these proteins.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge and citations

claim: Yap1/Taz interact with transcription factors such as the TEA domain family members Tead1-4 in the cell nucleus.
source: In the cell nucleus, Yap1/Taz interact with transcription factors, such as the TEA domain family members Tead1-4, and thereby regulate gene expression and promote growth processes (Yu and Guan, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu and Guan, 2013 and established scientific knowledge

claim: Enhanced expression and nuclear localization of Yap1/Taz were observed in multiple human cancers.
source: Accordingly, enhanced expression and nuclear localization of Yap1/Taz were observed in multiple human cancers (Moroishi et al., 2015) and inactivation of upstream Hippo signaling leads to tumor formation (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moroishi et al., 2015 and Lu et al., 2010

claim: Inactivation of upstream Hippo signaling leads to tumor formation.
source: Accordingly, enhanced expression and nuclear localization of Yap1/Taz were observed in multiple human cancers (Moroishi et al., 2015) and inactivation of upstream Hippo signaling leads to tumor formation (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lu et al., 2010

claim: Postnatal long bone contains extensive hypoxic areas compared to other organs such as brain, heart, lung, liver, spleen, or kidney.
source: In comparison to other organs, such as brain, heart, lung, liver, spleen, or kidney, postnatal long bone contains extensive hypoxic areas.
evidence: Supported by pimonidazole staining data presented in Figure 1A,B

claim: The metaphyseal region in proximity of the growth plate is less hypoxic than the secondary ossification center or the bone marrow in the diaphysis.
source: But even within long bone, pimonidazole (hypoxyprobe) staining or immunohistochemical analysis of the oxygen-controlled transcription factors hypoxia-inducible factor 1α (HIF-1α) and 2α (HIF-2α) uncover striking regional differences in oxygenation. The metaphyseal region in proximity of the growth plate is less hypoxic than the secondary ossification center (SOC) or the bone marrow in the diaphysis (bone shaft) (Figure 1A–D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by pimonidazole staining and HIF immunostaining data in Figure 1

claim: Endothelial marker genes such as Pecam1, Emcn, Cd34, Aplnr, Efnb2, and Esm1 are upregulated in mpECs relative to bmECs.
source: Endothelial marker genes such as Pecam1, Emcn, Cd34, Aplnr, Efnb2, and Esm1 are upregulated in mpECs relative to bmECs, whereas Kdr, Flt4, Tek, and Sele are downregulated (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E–G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: Transcripts for hypoxia-inducible transcription factors Hif1a and Epas1 (Hif2a) are upregulated in bmECs.
source: Consistent with the immunostaining results (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), transcripts for hypoxia-inducible transcription factors, namely Hif1a and Epas1 (Hif2a), and oxygen-controlled target genes are upregulated in bmECs (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1F

claim: Genes belonging to the glycolytic pathway are higher in bmECs than in mpECs.
source: In line with the regional differences in oxygenation, which are likely to limit the ability to metabolize fatty acids, genes belonging to the glycolytic pathway are higher in bmECs than in mpECs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I

claim: Target genes of Hippo signaling are upregulated in bmECs.
source: Our analysis also uncovered that target genes of Hippo signaling, an evolutionarily conserved pathway that promotes cell proliferation and organ growth, are upregulated in bmECs (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1G

claim: Yap1 immunostaining is more prominently visible in BM sinusoidal ECs in P21 femur sections.
source: In sections of P21 femur, immunostaining of Yes-associated protein 1 (Yap1), a transcriptional coregulatory in the Hippo signaling cascade, is more prominently visible in BM sinusoidal ECs, whereas expression in the metaphysis predominates in perivascular cells (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 1H

claim: Treatment of 3-week-old mice with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 for 3 hr profoundly increased endothelial and perivascular Yap1 and Taz protein signals in the metaphysis.
source: Treatment of 3-week-old mice with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 for 3 hr profoundly increased endothelial and perivascular Yap1 and Taz protein signals in the metaphysis but had relatively limited effects in the diaphysis (Figure 1I; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data after MG132 treatment presented in Figure 1I

claim: Strong phospho-Yap1S127 immunosignals can be seen in metaphyseal capillaries and associated perivascular cells.
source: Further arguing for rapid degradation of Yap1/Taz in the metaphysis, strong phospho-Yap1S127 immunosignals can be seen in metaphyseal capillaries and associated perivascular cells, which is accompanied by high expression of Lats2 protein in metaphyseal but not diaphyseal vessels (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D

claim: Yap1, Wwtr1, Lats1, and Lats2 transcripts are not significantly different between EC subsets.
source: In contrast, Yap1, Wwtr1, Lats1, and Lats2 transcripts are not significantly different between EC subsets (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E

claim: Inducible inactivation of Yap1 and Taz in postnatal ECs results in reduction of angiogenesis in the retinal vasculature.
source: While inducible inactivation of the two genes in postnatal ECs results in the expected reduction of angiogenesis in the retinal vasculature, vessel growth and the abundance of CD31hi Emcnhi ECs are significantly increased in long bone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in retina presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Inducible inactivation of Yap1 and Taz in postnatal ECs results in significantly increased vessel growth and abundance of CD31hi Emcnhi ECs in long bone.
source: While inducible inactivation of the two genes in postnatal ECs results in the expected reduction of angiogenesis in the retinal vasculature, vessel growth and the abundance of CD31hi Emcnhi ECs are significantly increased in long bone.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in bone presented in Figure 2

claim: EC-specific overexpression of a stabilized version of Yap1 impairs bone angiogenesis.
source: Furthermore, we show that Yap1/Taz negatively regulate the activity of the HIF pathway and thereby limit the expression of endothelial genes associated with vessel growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Yap1-KI mice presented in Figure 2G-L

claim: Inactivation of Lats2 impairs bone angiogenesis.
source: Furthermore, we show that Yap1/Taz negatively regulate the activity of the HIF pathway and thereby limit the expression of endothelial genes associated with vessel growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Lats2 mutant mice presented in Figure 3

claim: Yap1/Taz negatively regulate the activity of the HIF pathway.
source: Furthermore, we show that Yap1/Taz negatively regulate the activity of the HIF pathway and thereby limit the expression of endothelial genes associated with vessel growth.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq, ChIP, and cell culture data presented in Figures 4 and 5

claim: Yap1/TaziΔEC long bones at P21 display a much denser vessel network with more endothelial buds and columns relative to littermate controls.
source: Following administration of tamoxifen from postnatal day (P) 6–8, Yap1/TaziΔEC long bones at P21 display a much denser vessel network with more endothelial buds and column, a feature of actively growing bone vessels (Ramasamy et al., 2016a), relative to littermate controls (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2A,B

claim: The number of total ECs is significantly increased in P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone relative to littermate controls.
source: Furthermore, the number of total ECs, identified by Emcn immunostaining in combination with the Cdh5-mT/nG reporter, of Emcn+ EdU+ proliferating ECs, and of αSMA-covered arteries are significantly increased in P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone relative to littermate controls (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification data presented in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The number of Emcn+ EdU+ proliferating ECs is significantly increased in P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone relative to littermate controls.
source: Furthermore, the number of total ECs, identified by Emcn immunostaining in combination with the Cdh5-mT/nG reporter, of Emcn+ EdU+ proliferating ECs, and of αSMA-covered arteries are significantly increased in P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone relative to littermate controls (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data presented in Figure 2C,D

claim: The number of αSMA-covered arteries is significantly increased in P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone relative to littermate controls.
source: Furthermore, the number of total ECs, identified by Emcn immunostaining in combination with the Cdh5-mT/nG reporter, of Emcn+ EdU+ proliferating ECs, and of αSMA-covered arteries are significantly increased in P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone relative to littermate controls (Figure 2C,D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H

claim: The length of columnar vessels is increased in Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone.
source: The number of vessel buds and column in proximity of the growth plate and the length of columnar vessels, all of which are associated with vessel growth (Kusumbe et al., 2014; Ramasamy et al., 2016b), are also increased in Yap1/TaziΔEC long bone (Figure 2A,B,E,F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data presented in Figure 2F

claim: Vessel buds and columns are reduced in the Yap1-KIiEC metaphysis relative to littermate control.
source: Further arguing that Yap1/Taz play an unusual role as negative regulators of bone angiogenesis, Cdh5-CreERT2–controlled and thereby inducible overexpression of a stabilized version of Yap1 (Yap1S112A) in ECs (Yap1-KIiEC) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C) impairs growth of the bone vasculature. In P21 Yap1-KIiEC femur, distal vessel buds and arches, metaphyseal type H vessel columns, and EC proliferation are reduced (Figure 2G–L).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data presented in Figure 2G,H

claim: EC proliferation is reduced in P21 Yap1-KIiEC femur.
source: In P21 Yap1-KIiEC femur, distal vessel buds and arches, metaphyseal type H vessel columns, and EC proliferation are reduced (Figure 2G–L).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data presented in Figure 2K,L

claim: The absence of Lats2 in ECs causes a striking reduction of P21 femur and tibia length and weight.
source: The absence of Lats2 in ECs causes a striking reduction of P21 femur and tibia length and weight (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by measurements presented in Figure 3B,C

claim: Growth of the Lats2iΔEC long bone vasculature is strongly compromised.
source: Growth of the Lats2iΔEC long bone vasculature and vascularization of the secondary ossification center are strongly compromised, and vessel columns, distal buds as well as total type H ECs are significantly reduced compared to littermate controls (Figure 3D,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3D,E

claim: Yap1 and Taz are increased in Lats2iΔEC metaphyseal vessels.
source: In line with the role of Lats2 as a negative regulator of Yap1 and Taz, both proteins are increased in Lats2iΔEC metaphyseal vessels (Figure 3F,G; Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 3F,G

claim: mpEC proliferation is significantly reduced in Lats2iΔEC mutants.
source: In line with the reduction of Lats2iΔEC bone vessels, mpEC proliferation is significantly reduced, whereas apoptotic ECs are increased (Figure 3I–M).
evidence: Supported by EdU incorporation data presented in Figure 3I,J

claim: Apoptotic ECs are increased in Lats2iΔEC mutants.
source: In line with the reduction of Lats2iΔEC bone vessels, mpEC proliferation is significantly reduced, whereas apoptotic ECs are increased (Figure 3I–M).
evidence: Supported by active caspase-3 staining data presented in Figure 3K,L

claim: The outgrowth of the retinal vasculature is impaired in Yap1/TaziΔEC double mutant retinas.
source: Following the administration of tamoxifen from P1-P3, the outgrowth of the retinal vasculature, vessel sprouting and branching are impaired in Yap1/TaziΔEC double mutant retinas, which show strongly reduced EC numbers and significantly fewer proliferating (EdU+ Erg+) ECs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by retinal whole-mount staining data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C-E

claim: Lats2iΔEC mutants show strong defects in the bone vasculature but not in other organs such as retina, brain, liver, lung, kidney, heart, and spleen.
source: Lats2iΔEC mutants show strong defects in the bone vasculature but not in other organs such as retina, brain, liver, lung, kidney, heart, and spleen (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data of multiple organs presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: 341 genes are upregulated in Yap1/TaziΔEC mutant ECs.
source: Differential gene expression adjusted to a p-value of 0.05 identifies 341 upregulated genes and 118 downregulated genes in Yap1/TaziΔEC mutant ECs (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis presented in Figure 4A

claim: 118 genes are downregulated in Yap1/TaziΔEC mutant ECs.
source: Differential gene expression adjusted to a p-value of 0.05 identifies 341 upregulated genes and 118 downregulated genes in Yap1/TaziΔEC mutant ECs (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis presented in Figure 4A

claim: Biological processes such as angiogenesis, vascular development and EC migration are top hits among the genes that are upregulated in Yap1/TaziΔEC ECs.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis shows biological processes such as angiogenesis, vascular development and EC migration as top hits among the genes that are upregulated in Yap1/TaziΔEC ECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: The hypoxia-inducible factor transcription factor signaling networks are enriched in Yap1/TaziΔEC ECs.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) for cellular signaling pathways reveals that the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF1α and HIF2α) transcription factor signaling networks are enriched (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figure 4B

claim: HIF1α target genes such as Vegfa, Lrg1, Angtpl4, and Xbp1 are strongly upregulated in Yap1/TaziΔEC bone ECs.
source: In particular, HIF1α target genes and HIF-controlled pro-angiogenic genes, such as Vegfa, Lrg1, Angtpl4, and Xbp1, are strongly upregulated in Yap1/TaziΔEC bone ECs (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4C,D

claim: Expression of the Yap1/Taz controlled genes Cyr61, Thbs1, Ddah1, Lhfp, and Ctrg is increased in Lats2iΔEC ECs.
source: Consistent with the mutant phenotypes, expression of the Yap1/Taz controlled genes Cyr61, Thbs1, Ddah1, Lhfp, and Ctrg is increased in Lats2iΔEC ECs, whereas the HIF1α controlled genes Lrg1, Xbp1, Angptl4, and Vegfa are downregulated (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4E-G

claim: The HIF1α controlled genes Lrg1, Xbp1, Angptl4, and Vegfa are downregulated in Lats2iΔEC ECs.
source: Consistent with the mutant phenotypes, expression of the Yap1/Taz controlled genes Cyr61, Thbs1, Ddah1, Lhfp, and Ctrg is increased in Lats2iΔEC ECs, whereas the HIF1α controlled genes Lrg1, Xbp1, Angptl4, and Vegfa are downregulated (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 4E-G

claim: HUVECs grown under hypoxic (1% O2) conditions strongly upregulate VEGFA and ANGPTL4 expression relative to normoxia (21% O2).
source: HUVECs grown under hypoxic (1% O2) conditions strongly upregulate VEGFA and ANGPTL4 expression relative to normoxia (21% O2). Hypoxia also leads to strong upregulation of the Yap1/Taz target genes CTGF and CYR61 (Figure 5A) and, consistently, Yap1/Taz nuclear localization is increased under these conditions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from HUVEC culture presented in Figure 5A

claim: Hypoxia leads to strong upregulation of the Yap1/Taz target genes CTGF and CYR61 in HUVECs.
source: HUVECs grown under hypoxic (1% O2) conditions strongly upregulate VEGFA and ANGPTL4 expression relative to normoxia (21% O2). Hypoxia also leads to strong upregulation of the Yap1/Taz target genes CTGF and CYR61 (Figure 5A) and, consistently, Yap1/Taz nuclear localization is increased under these conditions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from HUVEC culture presented in Figure 5A

claim: Yap1/Taz nuclear localization is increased under hypoxic conditions in HUVECs.
source: Hypoxia also leads to strong upregulation of the Yap1/Taz target genes CTGF and CYR61 (Figure 5A) and, consistently, Yap1/Taz nuclear localization is increased under these conditions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data from HUVEC culture presented in Figure 5B

claim: Expression of the Hippo pathway target genes CTGF and CYR61 is strongly reduced in siYAP1/TAZ treated cells.
source: Expression of the Hippo pathway target genes CTGF and CYR61 is strongly reduced and the expression of the HIF1α target genes VEGFA and XBP1 are increased in siYAP1/TAZ treated cells (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from siRNA-treated HUVECs presented in Figure 5C

claim: Expression of the HIF1α target genes VEGFA and XBP1 are increased in siYAP1/TAZ treated cells.
source: Expression of the Hippo pathway target genes CTGF and CYR61 is strongly reduced and the expression of the HIF1α target genes VEGFA and XBP1 are increased in siYAP1/TAZ treated cells (Figure 5C; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from siRNA-treated HUVECs presented in Figure 5C

claim: HIF1α can be co-immunoprecipitated with Yap1/Taz proteins under hypoxic conditions.
source: Moreover, immunoprecipitation and Western blot experiments show that HIF1α can be co-immunoprecipitated with Yap1/Taz proteins under hypoxic conditions (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data presented in Figure 5D

claim: The HIF1α target genes VEGFA, ANPTL4, IGFBP2 and XBP1 are no longer upregulated after triple knockdown of HIF1A together with YAP1/TAZ.
source: Indeed, the HIF1α target genes VEGFA, ANPTL4, IGFBP2 and XBP1 are no longer upregulated after triple knockdown of HIF1A together with YAP1/TAZ (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from triple siRNA knockdown experiments presented in Figure 5E

claim: The binding of HIF1α to a hypoxia response element in the VEGFA gene is significantly increased after YAP1/TAZ knockdown.
source: Moreover, ChIP experiments show that the binding of HIF1α to a hypoxia response element in the VEGFA gene (position −947) is significantly increased after YAP1/TAZ knockdown (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data presented in Figure 5F

claim: EC-specific inactivation of the Hif1a gene impairs the expression of Vegfa and Angptl4 both in type H and type L ECs in vivo.
source: Highlighting the crosstalk between Yap1/Taz and HIF1α further, EC-specific inactivation of the Hif1a gene impairs the expression of Vegfa and Angptl4 both in type H and type L ECs in vivo, but it also reduces the expression of Ctgf and Cyr61 in type L cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from Hif1a mutant bone ECs presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D

claim: EC-specific expression of stabilized HIF1α increases the abundance of metaphyseal type H capillaries.
source: Cdh5-CreERT2-controlled and thereby EC-specific expression of a stabilized HIF1α mutant (Hif1AdPAiEC) lacking critical prolyl-hydroxylation sites (Kim et al., 2006) increases the abundance of metaphyseal type H capillaries, of columns and buds in proximity of the growth plate, and of arteries (Figure 6A–C), which is consistent with previously reported findings on the role of HIF signaling in bone ECs (Kusumbe et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data from HIF1AdPA mutants presented in Figure 6A-C

claim: The combination of Yap1/TaziΔEC and Hif1aiΔEC loss-of-function alleles normalizes the increase in bone vascularization seen in Yap1/TaziΔEC samples.
source: Supporting the crosstalk between Yap1/Taz and HIF-1α in vivo, the combination of Yap1/TaziΔEC and Hif1aiΔEC loss-of-function alleles normalizes the increase in bone vascularization seen in Yap1/TaziΔEC samples (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification data from double mutants presented in Figure 6D,E

claim: P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC mutant mice display slightly lower body weights than control littermates.
source: P21 Yap1/TaziΔEC mutant mice display slightly lower body weights than control littermates, whereas the length and weight of their femurs and tibias are not changed significantly (Figure 7A–C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by measurements presented in Figure 7A

claim: Osterix+ and Runx2+ osteoprogenitor cells are increased in the Yap1/TaziΔEC femur.
source: Osterix+ and Runx2+ osteoprogenitor cells and multiple indicators of bone formation, such as osteocalcin and the matrix proteins osteopontin and collagen type I, are increased in the Yap1/TaziΔEC femur (Figure 7D,E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: Trabecular bone fraction volume is significantly increased in Yap1/TaziΔEC femurs compared to littermate controls.
source: Micro-computed tomography (μCT) analysis of Yap1/TaziΔEC femurs demonstrated that these changes are accompanied by significant increases in trabecular bone (Tb) fraction volume, Tb number and thickness in comparison to littermate controls (Figure 7H,I).
evidence: Supported by μCT analysis presented in Figure 7H,I

claim: Trabecular spacing is reduced in Yap1/TaziΔEC samples.
source: Trabecular spacing, a parameter reflecting the separation of Tb elements, is reduced in Yap1/TaziΔEC samples.
evidence: Supported by μCT analysis presented in Figure 7I

claim: The number of osteoclasts is increased in Yap1/TaziΔEC mutants.
source: The number of osteoclasts, identified by antibodies directed against a subunit of vacuolar ATPase (ATP6V1B1/B2), is increased in mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) arguing that it is unlikely that the increase in trabecular bone is caused by impaired bone degradation.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B

claim: Body weight is reduced in P21 Yap1-KIiEC mutants.
source: Body weight as well as femoral and tibial length and weight is reduced in P21 Yap1-KIiEC mutants (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by measurements presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-E

claim: Expression of Yap1S112A leads to the reduction of Osterix+ osteoprogenitor cells.
source: Expression of Yap1S112A also leads to the reduction of Osterix+ osteoprogenitor cells and of osteopontin immunostaining (Figure 7F,G).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in Figure 7F,G

claim: The increase in Osterix+ cells seen after the loss of endothelial Yap1/Taz is restored to control level by the simultaneous and EC-specific inactivation of Hif1a.
source: The increase in Osterix+ cells seen after the loss of endothelial Yap1/Taz is restored to control level by the simultaneous and EC-specific inactivation of Hif1a (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data from double mutants presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F

claim: The loss of Yap1/Taz in ECs impairs endothelial proliferation and sprouting in the embryo and postnatal retina.
source: It was already shown that the loss of Yap1/Taz in ECs impairs endothelial proliferation and sprouting in the embryo and postnatal retina, whereas genetic gain-of-function experiments lead to endothelial hypersprouting and vascular hyperplasia (Kim et al., 2017; Neto et al., 2018; Sakabe et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2017; Neto et al., 2018; Sakabe et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017

claim: Genetic gain-of-function experiments of Yap1/Taz lead to endothelial hypersprouting and vascular hyperplasia.
source: It was already shown that the loss of Yap1/Taz in ECs impairs endothelial proliferation and sprouting in the embryo and postnatal retina, whereas genetic gain-of-function experiments lead to endothelial hypersprouting and vascular hyperplasia (Kim et al., 2017; Neto et al., 2018; Sakabe et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2017; Neto et al., 2018; Sakabe et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2017

claim: Taz has been linked to maladaptive effects such as the loss of quiescence, aberrant entry into the cell cycle and cell death in response to disturbed flow in ECs of the lymphatic system.
source: In ECs of the lymphatic system, Taz has been linked to maladaptive effects such as the loss of quiescence, aberrant entry into the cell cycle and, ultimately, cell death in response to disturbed flow (Sabine et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sabine et al., 2015

claim: Protective laminar flow suppresses Yap1/Taz activity in cultured ECs.
source: Likewise, while protective laminar flow suppresses Yap1/Taz activity in cultured ECs, exposure to disturbed flow led to the induction of Yap1/Taz-dependent proliferative and proinflammatory responses (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016

claim: Blood flow was identified as one of the upstream factors controlling the nuclear import of Yap1 in a Hippo-independent fashion in the zebrafish embryo.
source: In the zebrafish embryo, blood flow was also identified as one of the upstream factors controlling the nuclear import of Yap1 in a Hippo-independent fashion (Nakajima et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakajima et al., 2017

claim: Endothelial Yap1/Taz activity controls the expression of bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) and thereby transiently promotes intramembraneous ossification in the head of zebrafish embryos.
source: Another study has proposed that endothelial Yap1/Taz activity controls the expression of bone morphogenetic protein 4 (BMP4) and thereby transiently promotes intramembraneous ossification in the head of zebrafish embryos, while angiogenesis was unaffected (Uemura et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uemura et al., 2016

claim: Endothelial Notch signaling is a potent suppressor of angiogenesis in retina, brain and in tumors.
source: This is reminiscent of the role of endothelial Notch signaling, which is a potent suppressor of angiogenesis in retina, brain and in tumors (Benedito et al., 2012; Ridgway et al., 2006) but promotes type H formation, vessel growth and osteogenesis in long bone (Ramasamy et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Benedito et al., 2012; Ridgway et al., 2006

claim: Endothelial Notch signaling promotes type H formation, vessel growth and osteogenesis in long bone.
source: This is reminiscent of the role of endothelial Notch signaling, which is a potent suppressor of angiogenesis in retina, brain and in tumors (Benedito et al., 2012; Ridgway et al., 2006) but promotes type H formation, vessel growth and osteogenesis in long bone (Ramasamy et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramasamy et al., 2014

claim: Artery caliber, flow rates and calculated endothelial shear stress are comparably small inside bones relative to other tissues.
source: Artery caliber, flow rates and calculated endothelial shear stress are comparably small inside bones (Ramasamy et al., 2016b) relative to other tissues so that the impact of hemodynamic parameters might be more limited in bone ECs.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramasamy et al., 2016b and inference from data

claim: The observed nuclear localization of Yap1 in the sinusoidal endothelium is consistent with the previously reported flow-controlled regulation of Yap1/Taz.
source: Nevertheless, the observed nuclear localization of Yap1 in the sinusoidal endothelium, which has the lowest rates of flow (Bixel et al., 2017; Ramasamy et al., 2016b), is still consistent with the previously reported flow-controlled regulation of Yap1/Taz.
evidence: Based on inference from data and citations to Bixel et al., 2017; Ramasamy et al., 2016b

claim: Hypoxia is undetectable in the healthy retina and brain.
source: While hypoxia is undetectable in the healthy retina and brain (Kisler et al., 2017; Mezu-Ndubuisi et al., 2013), the interior of bone is highly hypoxic.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kisler et al., 2017; Mezu-Ndubuisi et al., 2013

claim: Live imaging in the adult murine calvarium showed the lowest local oxygen tension around the sinusoidal vasculature.
source: Live imaging in the adult murine calvarium showed the lowest local oxygen tension around the sinusoidal vasculature, whereas the endosteum is less hypoxic due to the presence of small arterioles (Spencer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spencer et al., 2014

claim: Type H ECs in the metaphysis show low steady state levels of Yap1/Taz consistent with the rapid, Hippo-dependent degradation of these proteins.
source: Type H ECs in the metaphysis show low steady state levels of Yap1/Taz consistent with the rapid, Hippo-dependent degradation of these proteins.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data showing proteasome inhibitor effects and phospho-Yap1 staining

claim: Higher levels of nuclear Yap1/Taz in the ECs of the diaphyseal vasculature might suppress excessive activation of the HIF pathway even though the local microenvironment is highly hypoxic.
source: In contrast, higher levels of nuclear Yap1/Taz in the ECs of the diaphyseal vasculature might suppress excessive activation of the HIF pathway even though the local microenvironment is highly hypoxic.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental data and proposed model

claim: Yap1 physically interacts with HIF1α in cultured cancer cell lines.
source: It was proposed that Yap1 physically interacts with HIF1α with in cultured cancer cell lines (Zhang et al., 2018), whereas HIF2α was shown was shown to enhance Yap1 activity without direct interaction of the two proteins (Jia et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: HIF2α enhances Yap1 activity without direct interaction of the two proteins.
source: It was proposed that Yap1 physically interacts with HIF1α with in cultured cancer cell lines (Zhang et al., 2018), whereas HIF2α was shown was shown to enhance Yap1 activity without direct interaction of the two proteins (Jia et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jia et al., 2019

claim: Hypoxia increases the stability of Yap1 by inducing the degradation of Lats2 through the E3 ubiquitin ligase SIAH2.
source: Furthermore, it was shown that hypoxia increases the stability of Yap1 by inducing the degradation of Lats2 through the E3 ubiquitin ligase SIAH2 (Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2015

claim: HIF1α and Yap1 can interact directly, leading to stabilization of HIF1α in cells cultured under hypoxic conditions.
source: The same study also proposed that HIF1α and Yap1 can interact directly, leading to stabilization of HIF1α in cells cultured under hypoxic conditions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma et al., 2015

claim: Yap1/Taz can act as transcriptional co-repressors and inhibit the expression of hypoxia-induced genes.
source: While these findings would not explain the observed repression of HIF1α activity in bone ECs, it was also reported that Yap1/Taz can act as transcriptional co-repressors and inhibit the expression of hypoxia-induced genes (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015
